title: Lesson 1: The Vertex Form of a Quadratic Function

blocks.alt: Two streams of water shoot from nozzles on a stone fountain rim and fall back into the basin. Each stream makes a smooth downward-opening arc; the highest point of each arc is visible against a park fence and trees.

blocks.text: Look at the water leaving the fountain. Each stream goes up and comes down.

blocks.prompt: Choose one stream. Mark the highest point of that stream — the place the water does not go above. Do not measure, and do not write an equation yet.

blocks.text: That turning point is the fact we will want from an equation of the curve. Vertex form is the writing that makes the high or low point readable.
A quadratic written as

is in vertex form. The vertex is the point \((h, k)\). The axis of symmetry is the vertical line \(x = h\). The sign of \(a\) tells you whether that vertex is a maximum or a minimum: negative \(a\) opens downward, so the vertex is a highest point; positive \(a\) opens upward, so the vertex is a lowest point.
Look at \(f(x) = (x + 3)^2 + 1\). The equation is already in vertex form, but notice the sign inside the brackets.

blocks.prompt: Where is the vertex? Write its coordinates before you check on the graph.

blocks.text: In this course, \(f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k\) is vertex form. The expanded writing \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) is standard form. Some books swap those names; this course does not.
Read the turning point from the equation
You named a vertex from a plus inside the brackets. Read this next equation the same way — vertex, axis, and whether the turning point is a maximum or a minimum.
Sketch a parabola that opens downward and turns at a point left of the origin and above the \(x\)-axis. Label that turning point. Draw a dashed vertical line through it.
The equation of that graph is
We need the vertex, the axis of symmetry, and whether the vertex is a maximum or a minimum.
Compare the equation with \(y = a(x - h)^2 + k\).
The brackets contain \((x + 2)\). Vertex form uses \((x - h)\), so rewrite \(x + 2\) as \(x - (-2)\). That makes \(h = -2\). The constant outside the brackets is \(+4\), so \(k = 4\).
The vertex is \((-2, 4)\). The axis of symmetry is the vertical line through the vertex, \(x = -2\).

The coefficient in front of the brackets is \(-3\). Because \(a\) is negative, the parabola opens downward, so the vertex is a maximum. The maximum value of the function is \(4\), and it occurs when \(x = -2\).
That highest point is the same kind of fact you marked on the water stream, now read from the writing.
A second equation, with nothing added outside
The last equation had a constant outside the brackets, so \(k\) was easy to see as a height. This Ontario sample includes
as one of the graphs to read from \(f(x) = x^2\). Use it here to inspect vertex form. (The sample also names \(g(x) = x^2 - 4\); stay with \(h(x)\).)
The brackets contain \((x + 1)\). Rewrite \(x + 1\) as \(x - (-1)\), so \(h = -1\). There is no constant added outside, so \(k = 0\). The vertex is \((-1, 0)\), and the axis is \(x = -1\).

The coefficient is \(-2\), so \(a\) is negative and the parabola opens downward. The vertex is a maximum even though \(k = 0\). Maximum versus minimum comes from the sign of \(a\), not from whether \(k\) looks positive.

blocks.prompt: Could you have decided maximum versus minimum from \(k\) on this equation? Say why or why not.

Do not move the graph yet. Keep the point you wrote. Then move the graph until it matches \(f(x) = (x + 3)^2 + 1\). Submit when the equation under the graph matches that writing.

blocks.prompt: Compare the vertex marker with the point you named. What in the equation told you the vertex? What did you have to change to match this writing?

blocks.text: Change only the horizontal position
The graph is back at \(f(x) = 2(x + 3)^2 + 1\). Do not move the graph yet.

blocks.prompt: If you change only \(h\) so the vertex sits at \(x = 2\), what will happen to the graph, and what will the new equation look like? Write that first.

blocks.text: Then move the graph so the vertex is at \(x = 2\), changing only \(h\) if you can. Submit. Say which quantity you meant to change: \(a\), \(h\), or \(k\).

blocks.prompt: Look at the equation under the graph and the dashed vertical line. What changed? What stayed the same? How do you read the new vertex from the equation?

blocks.text: The same curve, two writings
Vertex form makes the turning point easy to read. Expanding that writing into \(ax^2 + bx + c\) should not move the curve.
Sketch a parabola that opens upward, turning left of the origin and below the \(x\)-axis. Mark the vertex. A writing that fits that sketch is
The task is to write the same function as \(ax^2 + bx + c\), then check that both writings give the same outputs.
Square the binomial: \((x + 2)^2 = x^2 + 4x + 4\).
Multiply by \(a = \frac{1}{2}\): \(\frac{1}{2}x^2 + 2x + 2\).

Check a few inputs. At \(x = -2\), both writings give \(-3\). At \(x = 0\), both give \(-1\). At \(x = -4\), both give \(-1\). The table points sit on the same graph: expanding did not make a new parabola.

Now expand the starting equation from the graph, \(f(x) = 2(x + 3)^2 + 1\). If you rewrite it as \(ax^2 + bx + c\), will the graph be a different parabola or the same one? Write that down before you expand.
Expand on paper. Enter your \(b\) and \(c\) (\(a\) should stay 2), then submit. Do not copy an expanded line off the graph until after you have tried.

blocks.prompt: Do a few table points sit on both writings? If you plotted a second curve from your expanded coefficients, do the two graphs land on top of each other?

blocks.text: What this writing is for

You have been reading vertex form. Factored form \(f(x) = a(x - r)(x - s)\) makes the \(x\)-intercepts easy to see. Standard form \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) makes the \(y\)-intercept easy to see. Vertex form does not make those intercepts as obvious — and the vertex is not an intercept unless it actually sits on an axis.

blocks.prompt: What can you read from vertex form \(f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k\) that is harder to see when the same function is written as \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\)? Do not rewrite the function in another form.

blocks.text: Expand a new writing yourself

blocks.prompt: Given the vertex form \(f(x) = 3(x - 1)^2 + 4\), express the equation in standard form. Use technology to compare the graphs of these two forms of the equation.

blocks.text: Here, standard form means \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\). Expand the vertex form yourself first, then compare the graphs. Do not skip the expansion by only reading a line off the graph.
One more to try

If the graph is not available, work on paper with \(f(x) = 2(x + 3)^2 + 1\). First look at \(f(x) = (x + 3)^2 + 1\): name that vertex, then sketch both writings (same turning point, different stretch). From the starting equation, predict what happens if you change only \(h\) to 2; rewrite the equation and sketch again. Expand the starting equation yourself and check that a few table points still sit on the same sketch.

What the writing gives you

Vertex form \(f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k\) makes the vertex \((h, k)\) and the axis \(x = h\) readable. Maximum versus minimum comes from the sign of \(a\), not from the sign of \(k\) and not from which quadrant the vertex sits in.
Match the brackets to \((x - h)\). A plus inside the brackets does not mean the vertex is on the positive side of the \(x\)-axis.
\(a\) stretches or flips the graph. \(k\) moves the vertex up or down. Those two jobs are not the same.
Expanding vertex form into \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) gives the same parabola, not a new one. The graphs should land on top of each other.
